expectedText:
STAY-OR-PAY AND TRAINING REPAYMENT PROVISIONS AT TERMINATION (LABOR CODE § 926 / BUS. & PROF. CODE § 16608) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Corp.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Stay-or-Pay and Training Repayment Provisions at Termination — Information Sheet is prepared in connection with the employment relationship between Jane Doe and Acme Corp., and in particular a contract term described as: training-cost repayment agreement triggered if employment ends within 18 months. It describes what California Business and Professions Code section 16608 and Labor Code section 926 say about contract terms that require a worker to pay a debt, penalty, fee, or cost — or that trigger collection of one — because the worker's employment or work relationship with a specific employer terminates. These statutes apply only to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2026. This information sheet is not itself a determination that any specific term in any specific contract between Jane Doe and Acme Corp. is lawful, unlawful, void, or enforceable, and it does not resolve whether the amount at issue, stated here as $5,000, is or is not collectible.

CORE PROHIBITION ON TERMINATION-TRIGGERED DEBTS, FEES, AND PENALTIES
For a contract entered into on or after January 1, 2026, California Business and Professions Code section 16608 makes it unlawful to include in an employment contract — or to require a worker to sign, as a condition of employment or a work relationship, a separate contract that includes — a term that does any of three things: requires the worker to pay the employer, a training provider, or a debt collector for a debt because the worker's employment or work relationship with a specific employer terminates; authorizes the employer, training provider, or debt collector to resume or start collecting, or to end forbearance on, a debt for that same reason; or imposes any penalty, fee, or cost on the worker for that same reason. The statute reaches the contract term itself, regardless of which of the three mechanisms it uses, so long as termination of the work relationship with a specific employer is the trigger.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), for contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2026, it shall be unlawful to include in any employment contract, or to require a worker to execute as a condition of employment or a work relationship a contract that includes, a contract term that does any of the following:(A) Requires the worker to pay an employer, training provider, or debt collector for a debt if the worker’s employment or work relationship with a specific employer terminates.(B) Authorizes the employer, training provider, or debt collector to resume or initiate collection of or end forbearance on a debt if the worker’s employment or work relationship with a specific employer terminates.(C) Imposes any penalty, fee, or cost on a worker if the worker’s employment or work relationship with a specific employer terminates."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  Known gap: This prohibition is brand new: it applies only to contracts "entered into on or after January 1, 2026," so a materially identical repayment or fee provision in a contract signed before that date is not covered by this statute at all, and this clause takes no position on what law, if any, governs an earlier contract. The statute is limited to a contract term that is triggered by termination of the work relationship "with a specific employer" — its own text does not address a term triggered by some other event (for example, a fixed calendar date unrelated to separation, or a voluntary election unconnected to termination). Six statutory exceptions in subdivision (b)(2) narrow this prohibition and are addressed in this document's companion clauses rather than folded into this one. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(1)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

KEY DEFINITIONS: “DEBT,” “PENALTY, FEE, OR COST,” “WORKER,” AND “EMPLOYER”
Business and Professions Code section 16608 defines several terms broadly. “Debt” covers money, personal property, or their equivalent that is due, owing, or alleged to be due or owing from a natural person to another person — expressly including employment-related costs, education-related costs, or a consumer financial product or service — without regard to whether the debt is certain, contingent, or was incurred voluntarily. “Penalty, fee, or cost” is defined non-exclusively to include a replacement hire fee, retraining fee, replacement fee, quit fee, reimbursement for immigration or visa-related costs, liquidated damages, lost goodwill, and lost profit. “Worker” means a natural person permitted to work for or on behalf of an employer or business entity, or to participate in a work relationship, job training program, or skills training program, and is not limited to a common-law employee. “Employer” is likewise defined broadly to include any parent company, subsidiary, division, affiliate, contractor, hiring party, or third-party agent of an employer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Debt” means money, personal property, or their equivalent that is due or owing or alleged to be due or owing from a natural person to another person, including, but not limited to, for employment-related costs, education-related costs, or a consumer financial product or service, regardless of whether the debt is certain, contingent, or incurred voluntarily."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  "“Penalty, fee, or cost” includes, but is not limited to, a replacement hire fee, retraining fee, replacement fee, quit fee, reimbursement for immigration or visa-related costs, liquidated damages, lost goodwill, and lost profit."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(a)(7) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  "“Worker” means a natural person who is permitted to work for or on behalf of an employer or business entity, or who is permitted to participate in any other work relationship, job training program, or skills training program. “Worker” includes, but is not limited to, an employee or prospective employee."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(a)(11) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  "“Employer” means any person or entity that employs workers. “Employer” includes any parent company, subsidiary, division, affiliate, contractor, hiring party, or third-party agent of an employer."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  Known gap: These definitions apply "for purposes of this section" — they are not stated to govern how "debt," "worker," or "employer" are used elsewhere in the Business and Professions Code or the Labor Code. The definition of "debt" is deliberately broad and non-exclusive ("including, but not limited to"), and its own text does not resolve every close question about whether a specific charge, chargeback, or offset against final wages counts as a "debt" within its meaning. The statute separately defines “debt collector” by cross-reference to Civil Code section 1788.2(c), “freelance worker” by cross-reference to Section 18101, “misconduct” by cross-reference to Unemployment Insurance Code section 1256, and “transferable credential” and “training provider” with their own definitions; this clause quotes only the four terms most central to the prohibition and its trigger, not the full definitional list. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(a)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

VOIDNESS UNDER SECTION 16600 AND THE JANUARY 1, 2026 EFFECTIVE DATE
A contract term that is unlawful under Business and Professions Code section 16608(b) is treated as a contract restraining a person from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business — and is void under section 16600, California's general prohibition on non-compete agreements — but only if the contract was entered into on or after January 1, 2026. Labor Code section 926(a) states the same rule from the worker's side: a contract or contract term that violates section 16608 is void as contrary to public policy, again only if entered into on or after January 1, 2026.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(c) A contract that is unlawful under subdivision (b) is a contract restraining a person from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business, and is void under Section 16600 only if the contract was entered into on or after January 1, 2026."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  "(a) A contract or contract term that violates Section 16608 of the Business and Professions Code is void as contrary to public policy only if entered into on or after January 1, 2026."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 926(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=926)
  Known gap: Both statutes tie the voidness consequence expressly to the January 1, 2026 contracting date; neither statute's own text says what result follows for an identical provision in a contract entered into before that date, and this clause does not assume an answer to that question. The voidness rule operates through section 16600, so it inherits that section's general framework for void restraints of trade rather than creating a freestanding remedy of its own — the freestanding civil remedies are instead created separately by Labor Code section 926(b) and (c), addressed in this document's companion clause. This clause cites one subdivision from each of two statutes (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(c) and Lab. Code § 926(a)); each was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

EXCEPTION: TUITION REPAYMENT FOR A TRANSFERABLE CREDENTIAL
Section 16608(b)(2)(B) exempts a contract for repayment of tuition costs for a “transferable credential” — defined elsewhere in the statute as a degree offered by an accredited third-party institution that is not required for the worker's current job and is transferable and useful for employment beyond the current employer — but only if five conditions are all met: the repayment contract is offered separately from the employment contract; obtaining the credential is not made a condition of employment; the repayment amount is specified before the worker agrees and does not exceed the employer's actual cost of the credential; any required-employment period comes with a repayment amount that is prorated to the length of that period, without an accelerated payment schedule on separation; and the worker does not owe repayment if terminated, unless the termination was for misconduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(B) A contract related to the repayment of the cost of tuition for a transferable credential that meets all of the following requirements:(i) The contract is offered separately from any contract for employment.(ii) The contract does not require obtaining the transferable credential as a condition of employment. (iii) The contract specifies the repayment amount before the worker agrees to the contract, and the repayment amount does not exceed the cost to the employer of the transferable credential received by the worker.(iv) The contract provides for a prorated repayment amount during any required employment period that is proportional to the total repayment amount and the length of the required employment period and does not require an accelerated payment schedule if the worker separates from the employment.(v) The contract does not require repayment to the employer by the worker if the worker is terminated, except if the worker is terminated for misconduct."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  Known gap: This exception applies only to a “transferable credential” as the statute defines it — a third-party-institution degree not required for the worker's current employment — and its own text does not extend to repayment of costs for a certification, license, or in-house training program that does not meet that specific definition; those may instead fall under the separate signing-bonus/retention-payment exception in subdivision (b)(2)(D) or under no exception at all. All five listed requirements must be met; the statute's own text does not say what happens to a contract that satisfies some but not all of them, and this clause does not resolve that question. “Misconduct” for purposes of the termination carve-out in (v) is defined by cross-reference to Unemployment Insurance Code section 1256, addressed separately in this corpus's unemployment insurance disqualification materials rather than repeated here. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(B)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

EXCEPTION: DISCRETIONARY SIGNING BONUS WITH A RETENTION PERIOD
Section 16608(b)(2)(D) exempts a contract for a discretionary or unearned monetary payment — including a financial bonus — paid at the outset of employment and not tied to specific job performance, provided five conditions are all met: the repayment terms are in a separate agreement from the main employment contract; the worker is notified of the right to consult an attorney and given at least five business days to do so before signing; any repayment obligation for early separation carries no interest and is prorated to the remaining term of a retention period capped at two years from receipt of the payment; the worker has the option to defer receiving the payment until the retention period is fully served, with no repayment obligation in that case; and the separation that would trigger repayment must have been at the worker's own sole election, or at the employer's election for misconduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(D) A contract for the receipt of a discretionary or unearned monetary payment, including a financial bonus, at the outset of employment that is not tied to specific job performance, provided that all of the following conditions are met:(i) The terms of any repayment obligation are set forth in a separate agreement from the primary employment contract.(ii) The employee is notified that they have the right to consult an attorney regarding the agreement and provided with a reasonable time period of not less than five business days to obtain advice of counsel prior to executing the agreement.(iii) Any repayment obligation for early separation from employment is not subject to interest accrual and is prorated based on the remaining term of any retention period, which shall not exceed two years from the receipt of payment.(iv) The worker has an option to defer receipt of the payment to the end of a fully served retention period without any repayment obligation.(v) Separation from employment prior to the retention period was at the sole election of the employee, or at the election of the employer for misconduct."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(D) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  Known gap: This exception is narrower than a general “signing bonus clawback” exception: it requires the payment to be discretionary or unearned and not tied to job performance, the repayment terms to be in a document separate from the employment contract, an advance attorney-consultation notice of at least five business days, no interest on repayment, proration to the remaining retention period, a retention period capped at two years, a deferral option, and a separation trigger limited to the worker's own election or an employer election for misconduct — all eight elements together, not any one of them alone. The statute's own text does not say what result follows for a bonus-repayment arrangement that satisfies most but not all of these conditions. Whether a specific payment is “discretionary or unearned” and “not tied to specific job performance” is a fact-specific characterization this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(D)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

THREE FURTHER EXCEPTIONS: GOVERNMENT LOAN PROGRAMS, APPRENTICESHIPS, AND RESIDENTIAL PROPERTY CONTRACTS
Section 16608(b)(2) exempts three further categories of contract from the core prohibition, in addition to the transferable-credential and discretionary-bonus exceptions addressed separately in this document. First, a contract entered into under any loan repayment assistance program or loan forgiveness program provided by a federal, state, or local governmental agency is not covered. Second, a contract related to enrollment in an apprenticeship program approved by California's Division of Apprenticeship Standards is not covered. Third, a contract related to the lease, financing, or purchase of residential property — including, but not limited to, a contract under the California Residential Mortgage Lending Act — is not covered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(A) A contract entered into under any loan repayment assistance program or loan forgiveness program provided by a federal, state, or local governmental agency."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  "(C) A contract related to enrollment in an apprenticeship program approved by the Division of Apprenticeship Standards."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(C) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  "(E) A contract related to the lease, financing, or purchase of residential property, including, but not limited to, a contract pursuant to the California Residential Mortgage Lending Act (Division 20 (commencing with Section 50000) of the Financial Code)."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(E) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  Known gap: Each of these three exceptions is stated without the multi-factor conditions attached to the transferable-credential and discretionary-bonus exceptions — the statute's own text imposes no separate list of requirements on a loan-forgiveness-program contract, an approved-apprenticeship contract, or a residential-property contract for the exception to apply. The apprenticeship exception turns on approval by the Division of Apprenticeship Standards specifically; the statute's own text does not address an unapproved or informally structured apprenticeship arrangement. The residential-property exception is illustrated, not limited, by its cross-reference to the California Residential Mortgage Lending Act (“including, but not limited to”), and this document does not attempt to catalog every residential-property financing arrangement the exception might reach. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(A), (C), and (E)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

PRIVATE CIVIL ACTION, STATUTORY DAMAGES, AND ATTORNEY'S FEES
Labor Code section 926(b) authorizes a worker subjected to the conduct prohibited by section 16608(b) of the Business and Professions Code, or a worker representative, to bring a civil action on behalf of that worker, other similarly situated persons, or both, in any court of competent jurisdiction. Section 926(c) states that a person found liable is liable for the worker's or workers' actual damages, or $5,000 per worker, whichever is greater, in addition to injunctive relief and reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) A worker who has been subjected to the conduct prohibited by subdivision (b) of Section 16608 of the Business and Professions Code or a worker representative may bring a civil action on behalf of that worker, other persons similarly situated, or both, in any court of competent jurisdiction."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 926(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=926)
  "(c) Any person found liable for a violation of this section shall be liable for actual damages sustained by the worker or workers on whose behalf the case is brought, or five thousand dollars ($5,000) per worker, whichever is greater, in addition to injunctive relief, and reasonable attorney’s fees and costs."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 926(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=926)
  Known gap: The statute creates a per-worker damages floor of $5,000 that applies only “or,” as an alternative to actual damages, whichever amount is greater — it does not stack the two. Section 926(b) authorizes an action “on behalf of” other similarly situated persons; the statute's own text does not specify class-certification or representative-action procedures beyond that grant, and this document does not describe how such an action would be litigated. “Worker representative” is not further defined in section 926 itself. This clause cites two subdivisions of a single statutory section (Lab. Code § 926(b) and (c)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

CUMULATIVE WITH OTHER RIGHTS — EXPENSE REIMBURSEMENT, WORKER CLASSIFICATION, AND UNFAIR COMPETITION LAW
Business and Professions Code section 16608(d) states that the rights, remedies, and penalties it establishes are cumulative and do not supersede or limit rights, remedies, or penalties available under other law — naming, by way of example, an employer's business-expense reimbursement obligations under Labor Code section 2802, the worker-classification provisions beginning at Labor Code section 2775, and the Unfair Competition Law beginning at Business and Professions Code section 17200. Labor Code section 926(d) states the reciprocal rule: section 926 does not limit the remedies otherwise available to a worker or other natural person under section 16608.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(d) The rights, remedies, and penalties established by this section are cumulative and shall not be construed to supersede or limit the rights, remedies, or penalties established under other laws, or to limit the ability of any other person or entity to pursue enforcement of rights, remedies, or penalties established under other laws, including, but not limited to:(1) Obligations of employers under Section 2802 of the Labor Code.(2) Article 1.5 (commencing with Section 2775) of Chapter 2 of Division 3 of the Labor Code.(3) The Unfair Competition Law (Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200))."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16608)
  "(d) This section does not limit the remedies available to a worker or other natural person specified in Section 16608 of the Business and Professions Code."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 926(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=926)
  Known gap: Subdivision (d)'s list of other laws is introduced by “including, but not limited to,” so the three named provisions illustrate rather than exhaust the other legal theories that might independently apply to the same underlying facts; this document does not attempt a complete cross-reference. Whether a specific reimbursement dispute, misclassification claim, or unfair-competition claim actually applies to any given contract term is governed by those separate bodies of law, addressed in this corpus's own dedicated materials on those subjects rather than repeated here. This clause cites one subdivision from each of two statutes (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(d) and Lab. Code § 926(d)); each was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

The voidness rule operates through section 16600, so it inherits that section's general framework for void restraints of trade rather than creating a freestanding remedy of its own — the freestanding civil remedies are instead created separately by Labor Code section 926(b) and (c), addressed in this document's companion clause. This clause cites one subdivision from each of two statutes (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(c) and Lab. Code § 926(a)); each was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

expectedJSON.body: Section 16608(b)(2)(B) exempts a contract for repayment of tuition costs for a “transferable credential” — defined elsewhere in the statute as a degree offered by an accredited third-party institution that is not required for the worker's current job and is transferable and useful for employment beyond the current employer — but only if five conditions are all met: the repayment contract is offered separately from the employment contract; obtaining the credential is not made a condition of employment; the repayment amount is specified before the worker agrees and does not exceed the employer's actual cost of the credential; any required-employment period comes with a repayment amount that is prorated to the length of that period, without an accelerated payment schedule on separation; and the worker does not owe repayment if terminated, unless the termination was for misconduct.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (B) A contract related to the repayment of the cost of tuition for a transferable credential that meets all of the following requirements:(i) The contract is offered separately from any contract for employment.(ii) The contract does not require obtaining the transferable credential as a condition of employment. (iii) The contract specifies the repayment amount before the worker agrees to the contract, and the repayment amount does not exceed the cost to the employer of the transferable credential received by the worker.(iv) The contract provides for a prorated repayment amount during any required employment period that is proportional to the total repayment amount and the length of the required employment period and does not require an accelerated payment schedule if the worker separates from the employment.(v) The contract does not require repayment to the employer by the worker if the worker is terminated, except if the worker is terminated for misconduct.

expectedJSON.gap: This exception applies only to a “transferable credential” as the statute defines it — a third-party-institution degree not required for the worker's current employment — and its own text does not extend to repayment of costs for a certification, license, or in-house training program that does not meet that specific definition; those may instead fall under the separate signing-bonus/retention-payment exception in subdivision (b)(2)(D) or under no exception at all. All five listed requirements must be met; the statute's own text does not say what happens to a contract that satisfies some but not all of them, and this clause does not resolve that question. “Misconduct” for purposes of the termination carve-out in (v) is defined by cross-reference to Unemployment Insurance Code section 1256, addressed separately in this corpus's unemployment insurance disqualification materials rather than repeated here. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(B)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

expectedJSON.body: Section 16608(b)(2)(D) exempts a contract for a discretionary or unearned monetary payment — including a financial bonus — paid at the outset of employment and not tied to specific job performance, provided five conditions are all met: the repayment terms are in a separate agreement from the main employment contract; the worker is notified of the right to consult an attorney and given at least five business days to do so before signing; any repayment obligation for early separation carries no interest and is prorated to the remaining term of a retention period capped at two years from receipt of the payment; the worker has the option to defer receiving the payment until the retention period is fully served, with no repayment obligation in that case; and the separation that would trigger repayment must have been at the worker's own sole election, or at the employer's election for misconduct.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(D) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (D) A contract for the receipt of a discretionary or unearned monetary payment, including a financial bonus, at the outset of employment that is not tied to specific job performance, provided that all of the following conditions are met:(i) The terms of any repayment obligation are set forth in a separate agreement from the primary employment contract.(ii) The employee is notified that they have the right to consult an attorney regarding the agreement and provided with a reasonable time period of not less than five business days to obtain advice of counsel prior to executing the agreement.(iii) Any repayment obligation for early separation from employment is not subject to interest accrual and is prorated based on the remaining term of any retention period, which shall not exceed two years from the receipt of payment.(iv) The worker has an option to defer receipt of the payment to the end of a fully served retention period without any repayment obligation.(v) Separation from employment prior to the retention period was at the sole election of the employee, or at the election of the employer for misconduct.

expectedJSON.gap: This exception is narrower than a general “signing bonus clawback” exception: it requires the payment to be discretionary or unearned and not tied to job performance, the repayment terms to be in a document separate from the employment contract, an advance attorney-consultation notice of at least five business days, no interest on repayment, proration to the remaining retention period, a retention period capped at two years, a deferral option, and a separation trigger limited to the worker's own election or an employer election for misconduct — all eight elements together, not any one of them alone. The statute's own text does not say what result follows for a bonus-repayment arrangement that satisfies most but not all of these conditions. Whether a specific payment is “discretionary or unearned” and “not tied to specific job performance” is a fact-specific characterization this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(D)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

expectedJSON.body: Section 16608(b)(2) exempts three further categories of contract from the core prohibition, in addition to the transferable-credential and discretionary-bonus exceptions addressed separately in this document. First, a contract entered into under any loan repayment assistance program or loan forgiveness program provided by a federal, state, or local governmental agency is not covered. Second, a contract related to enrollment in an apprenticeship program approved by California's Division of Apprenticeship Standards is not covered. Third, a contract related to the lease, financing, or purchase of residential property — including, but not limited to, a contract under the California Residential Mortgage Lending Act — is not covered.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (A) A contract entered into under any loan repayment assistance program or loan forgiveness program provided by a federal, state, or local governmental agency.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(C) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (C) A contract related to enrollment in an apprenticeship program approved by the Division of Apprenticeship Standards.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(E) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (E) A contract related to the lease, financing, or purchase of residential property, including, but not limited to, a contract pursuant to the California Residential Mortgage Lending Act (Division 20 (commencing with Section 50000) of the Financial Code).

expectedJSON.gap: Each of these three exceptions is stated without the multi-factor conditions attached to the transferable-credential and discretionary-bonus exceptions — the statute's own text imposes no separate list of requirements on a loan-forgiveness-program contract, an approved-apprenticeship contract, or a residential-property contract for the exception to apply. The apprenticeship exception turns on approval by the Division of Apprenticeship Standards specifically; the statute's own text does not address an unapproved or informally structured apprenticeship arrangement. The residential-property exception is illustrated, not limited, by its cross-reference to the California Residential Mortgage Lending Act (“including, but not limited to”), and this document does not attempt to catalog every residential-property financing arrangement the exception might reach. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(A), (C), and (E)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code section 926(b) authorizes a worker subjected to the conduct prohibited by section 16608(b) of the Business and Professions Code, or a worker representative, to bring a civil action on behalf of that worker, other similarly situated persons, or both, in any court of competent jurisdiction. Section 926(c) states that a person found liable is liable for the worker's or workers' actual damages, or $5,000 per worker, whichever is greater, in addition to injunctive relief and reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 926(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (b) A worker who has been subjected to the conduct prohibited by subdivision (b) of Section 16608 of the Business and Professions Code or a worker representative may bring a civil action on behalf of that worker, other persons similarly situated, or both, in any court of competent jurisdiction.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 926(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (c) Any person found liable for a violation of this section shall be liable for actual damages sustained by the worker or workers on whose behalf the case is brought, or five thousand dollars ($5,000) per worker, whichever is greater, in addition to injunctive relief, and reasonable attorney’s fees and costs.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute creates a per-worker damages floor of $5,000 that applies only “or,” as an alternative to actual damages, whichever amount is greater — it does not stack the two. Section 926(b) authorizes an action “on behalf of” other similarly situated persons; the statute's own text does not specify class-certification or representative-action procedures beyond that grant, and this document does not describe how such an action would be litigated. “Worker representative” is not further defined in section 926 itself. This clause cites two subdivisions of a single statutory section (Lab. Code § 926(b) and (c)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

expectedJSON.body: Business and Professions Code section 16608(d) states that the rights, remedies, and penalties it establishes are cumulative and do not supersede or limit rights, remedies, or penalties available under other law — naming, by way of example, an employer's business-expense reimbursement obligations under Labor Code section 2802, the worker-classification provisions beginning at Labor Code section 2775, and the Unfair Competition Law beginning at Business and Professions Code section 17200. Labor Code section 926(d) states the reciprocal rule: section 926 does not limit the remedies otherwise available to a worker or other natural person under section 16608.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (d) The rights, remedies, and penalties established by this section are cumulative and shall not be construed to supersede or limit the rights, remedies, or penalties established under other laws, or to limit the ability of any other person or entity to pursue enforcement of rights, remedies, or penalties established under other laws, including, but not limited to:(1) Obligations of employers under Section 2802 of the Labor Code.(2) Article 1.5 (commencing with Section 2775) of Chapter 2 of Division 3 of the Labor Code.(3) The Unfair Competition Law (Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200)).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 926(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (d) This section does not limit the remedies available to a worker or other natural person specified in Section 16608 of the Business and Professions Code.

expectedJSON.gap: Subdivision (d)'s list of other laws is introduced by “including, but not limited to,” so the three named provisions illustrate rather than exhaust the other legal theories that might independently apply to the same underlying facts; this document does not attempt a complete cross-reference. Whether a specific reimbursement dispute, misclassification claim, or unfair-competition claim actually applies to any given contract term is governed by those separate bodies of law, addressed in this corpus's own dedicated materials on those subjects rather than repeated here. This clause cites one subdivision from each of two statutes (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(d) and Lab. Code § 926(d)); each was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.
